series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/6] mm/compaction: wait for pfn walkers before poisoning offlined memmap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a bug in the Linux kernel's compaction module where it fails to wait for pfn walkers before poisoning offlined memory maps, leading to DEBUG_VM faults. The fix involves holding an SRCU-fast read section from block check to last use of pages and making remove_pfn_range_from_zone() clear zone->contiguous and wait before poisoning. This patch also takes into account the contiguous zone skipping online checks and ensures scanner positions outlive the section.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/6] mm/page_owner: hold off memory offline while a page is read
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents memory offline operations from interfering with the reading of page ownership information in /sys/kernel/debug/page_owner. It does this by moving the check for online pages inside a read section and reordering code to avoid sleeping locks while holding hotplug locks. This fix addresses an issue where reading page owner information could cause kernel oops when memory is being removed or offline.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/6] mm/memory-failure: keep the page online while handling it
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the memory-failure handling in the Linux kernel to keep a page online while it is being handled, preventing potential faults and crashes due to the page going offline during processing. The change involves moving the get_online_mems() call earlier in the code to ensure that the page remains online until its use is complete. This fix addresses issues with memory failure handling, particularly when dealing with poisoned pages, and has been tested to prevent faults and maintain lockdep cleanliness.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/6] mm/page_alloc: don't undo another isolation in alloc_contig_range
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents alloc_contig_range from undoing another isolation in the range when it fails, which can cause an offline device to spin indefinitely holding a hotplug lock. The problem occurs when alloc_contig_range overlaps a block going offline and isolates its own blocks, but fails due to EBUSY on CPU 1's blocks. This patch fixes this issue by returning directly from alloc_contig_frozen_range_noprof when isolation fails, rather than undoing the isolation over the whole range. The approach taken is to modify the logic in alloc_contig_frozen_range_noprof to handle the case where isolation fails and another caller has isolated blocks in the range.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/6] mm/page_alloc: keep the range online while alloc_contig isolates it
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a bug where a gigantic hugetlb allocation can crash due to a range going offline while being isolated by alloc_contig_pages(). The patch adds a check that the range is online before isolating it, and then looks up the zone only after isolation. This prevents the range from going offline during isolation, which was causing crashes when memory was removed concurrently.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 6/6] mm/hwpoison-inject: keep the page online while filtering it
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the hwpoison-inject module where injecting a memory error while filtering it and the memory is hot-removed can cause a crash. The issue occurs because the filter can sleep, causing the page to be offline when the memory is removed. To fix this, the patch adds a lock around the filter check using get_online_mems() and checks if the pfn is valid under this lock. This ensures that the page remains online while filtering it, preventing the crash.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses six races in the Linux kernel's memory management code that can cause crashes or incorrect behavior when memory is offline. The patches introduce a new function, pfn_walk, which waits for pending page walkers before poisoning the memory map, and modify various functions to use this new function or hold get_online_mems() instead. This ensures that memory is not accessed after it has been marked as offline, preventing crashes and incorrect behavior. The changes are tested on a QEMU guest with three NUMA nodes and a pc-dimm left offline at boot, and the results show that the patches fix all six races without introducing any significant performance cost.

I actually have a reason for these fixes other than "bot said bad".

We leverage ballooning and hotplugging as VM memory overcommit tools
and are finding that some of these race conditions crash them with
large MTBF.

While most of these are insanely narrow, they are not as unlikely to
happen as you think. A vCPU can take a vmexit in these windows much
more easily than a host can take an NMI or other interrupt.

Thankfully none of these (or the other series) appear to be obvious
security issues, but they are stability issues.

I have a reproducer for every single one of these (and the other
series) - but a handful are unreachable due to a 2-statement read
being emitted as a single read by the compiler (which can be undone
by a targeted compiler flag). Those were included for completeness.

structurally, but it uses SRCU-fast on the fast path. The catch is that
PowerPC (and i think others?) don't SRCU-fast without atomics, so they
take a performance hit.  (It also doesn't help us for backports)

I've been weighing that solution over never freeing and/or prepopulating
zones - but this also results in performance impacts (leaving dead zones
in the list forces the allocator to walk them for no value).

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch updates the automatic interleave weights in Linux's memory policy when a node gains or loses memory due to hotplug events. The current implementation only recalculates the weights when a new bandwidth is reported, which can lead to incorrect weights being used for some nodes. This patch introduces a new function `wi_state_refresh` that recomputes the weights from the recorded bandwidth whenever a node gains its first memory or loses its last. This ensures that the weighted interleave algorithm always uses accurate and up-to-date weights, leading to improved performance in certain scenarios.

patches_acked.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue where the userfaultfd registration mode is not properly updated when changing from MISSING|WP to WP, leading to missing pages still waiting for userspace access. series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the exportfs and mountd modules to track the highest attribute in the kernel's svc_export netlink policy, which is used to determine what attributes should be sent to older kernels that may reject them. The patch adds a new field 'max_attr' to the nfsd_export_policy structure and populates it with the maximum attribute value from the policy. This change is necessary to avoid sending attributes that an older kernel would reject, causing the whole entry to be rejected. The patch also updates the exportfs module's logging to include the maximum attribute value.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for riomode= and wiomode= export options to the NFS exports system. These options allow users to specify how I/O operations are handled by the kernel, and can be used to improve performance or reduce latency. The patch also includes changes to handle kernels that do not support these options, and updates various files to reflect the new functionality. Specifically, it adds a function to check if the running kernel supports riomode/wiomode, and modifies the mountd daemon to drop these options on unsupported kernels instead of leaving the export unmountable.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a tool called nfsd-iomode-advisor that recommends the optimal NFSD IO mode (buffered, dontcache, or direct) for an export based on various metrics and thresholds. The tool samples performance metrics while clients use the export and provides recommendations with reasons. It considers factors such as miss ratio, reclaim vs storage traffic, CPU time of kswapd/kcompactd threads, dirty/writeback ratios, free memory vs zone high watermarks, and average READ/WRITE sizes. The tool also probes for mode limits and caveats, ensuring that the recommended mode is suitable for the export's characteristics and does not silently fall back to a different mode.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patchset adds support for two new export options, riomode= and wiomode=, to the Linux NFS server. These options allow administrators to specify the I/O mode for an exported file system, which can improve performance by matching the I/O characteristics of the client with the capabilities of the server. The patch also includes a script called nfsd-iomode-advisor that provides recommendations for choosing the optimal I/O mode based on various server statistics. This is intended to be a companion patchset to another submission that adds support for tracking the service export policy highest attribute.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/6] NFSD: Add per-export read/write I/O mode settings
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds per-export read/write I/O mode settings to the NFS server (NFSD). It introduces two new fields, `ex_riomode` and `ex_wiomode`, in the `struct svc_export` structure. These fields are used to store the I/O modes for reading and writing, respectively. The patch also updates the netlink specification to include these new fields and adds policy checks to ensure their validity. Additionally, it modifies the cache update logic to copy the settings from the netlink attributes to the export's internal state. This allows administrators to configure different I/O modes for each export on a per-export basis.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/6] NFSD: Apply per-export I/O modes to READ and WRITE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the NFS server to apply per-export I/O modes for READ and WRITE operations. It resolves each export's effective I/O mode by considering both explicit settings and the global io_cache_read/write knob. The patch also skips splice for reads on exports whose effective read mode is not buffered. Additionally, it updates the debugfs knob comments to match the new behavior.

the global knob is switched to dontcache or direct, so

reached. An export pinned to riomode=buffered on such a server never
gets splice; it falls through to nfsd_iter_read() and does vector
buffered reads. The same applies to the splice_ok decisions in

IO mode "regardless of the global knob", and that isn't quite true
now for the buffered case.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/6] NFSD: Keep per-export statistics across export cache updates
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where NFS statistics are lost when an export cache entry is replaced or removed. To solve this, it introduces a per-net table to store statistics keyed on the export root and client name. Each export cache entry takes a reference to the shared statistics in svc_export_init() and drops it when freed. Statistics that have not been used for an hour are automatically freed by a delayed work item. This approach ensures that statistics are preserved across export cache updates, allowing tools to accurately track traffic over intervals.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/6] NFSD: Count the storage reads of each export's READs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new counter to track the storage reads of each export in NFS, which is essential for determining the optimal I/O mode for an export. The current implementation only reports bytes returned by READ operations, but this can be misleading as it includes page cache hits and other factors. To address this issue, the patch introduces a new io_read_storage counter that captures the actual storage reads initiated by each export's READ operations. This counter is only visible when CONFIG_TASK_IO_ACCOUNTING is enabled. The patch modifies several files to implement this new feature, including export.c, export.h, stats.h, and vfs.c.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 6/6] NFSD: Document how to choose an IO mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds documentation to help administrators choose the correct IO mode for an NFS export, including when to use buffered, dontcache, or direct IO. It explains why a low server page cache hit rate is normal and lists workload conditions that favor each IO mode. The documentation also describes existing metrics to measure performance, such as per-export miss ratio from export_stats and client mountstats byte counters.

A companion patchset in nfs-utils will add support for these options and provide tools to help users configure them.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm/huge_memory: scale thp_underused() to the folio size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the thp_underused() function to be aware of the size of a folio, rather than assuming it's always PMD-sized. It scales the khugepaged_max_ptes_none threshold proportionally to the number of pages in the folio, ensuring that the same fraction of zero-filled pages is tolerated regardless of folio size. This change will prevent issues when collapsing mTHP orders and splitting folios, as both operations would use the same threshold for a given folio size. The patch makes no functional changes for PMD-sized folios, as their nr_pages value remains HPAGE_PMD_NR.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios when underused splitting is inactive
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the huge_memory module to skip queueing folios for underused splitting when the khugepaged/max_ptes_none sysctl is at its maximum, which is the default setting. This change optimizes performance by avoiding unnecessary work on anonymous PMD-sized folios that are mostly zero-filled. The patch also introduces a new function thp_underused_never() to factor out this check and share it between deferred_split_folio() and thp_underused().

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau
review_comments.summary: Approved the patch with a Reviewed-by tag, indicating that it meets kernel coding standards and is ready for merge.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Oct 23, 2026 at 04:00:05PM -0700, Joanne Koong wrote:
> Every anonymous PMD-sized folio is put on the deferred split queue when
> it is first mapped, so that the shrinker can find it under memory
> pressure and split it if it turns out to be mostly zero-filled.
> 
> With the default khugepaged/max_ptes_none this is wasted work. The
> default is HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1, which tells thp_underused() that any number
> of zero-filled pages is tolerable, which means the shrinker will never
> split any of these folios for being underused. They take the list_lru
> lock at fault time, inflate the object count the shrinker reports, and
> are then walked and dropped when they're first scanned.
> 
> Skip the queueing when khugepaged/max_ptes_none is at its maximum, and
> factor that check out into thp_underused_never() so that
> deferred_split_folio() and thp_underused() share it. Since the default
> is the maximum, out of the box no folio is queued for underused
> splitting at all, PMD-sized ones included. Partially mapped folios are
> still queued as before.
> 
> This also matters for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios
> to the deferred split list, as it keeps systems running the default from
> paying for that on every anonymous fault.
> 
> Please note that the queue has always been best-effort. A folio that was
> queued before khugepaged/max_ptes_none is lowered gets dropped from the
> queue by the first scan that finds it's not underused, so changing the
> sysctl has never retroactively applied to folios that were already
> scanned. Requeueing eligible folios when the sysctl changes will be
> addressed in a separate patch.
> 
> Suggested-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>
> Suggested-by: David Hildenbrand <david@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>

Reviewed-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, allowing them to be split and reclaimed when under memory pressure. This addresses a problem where fully mapped mTHP folios that are mostly zero-filled were not being split due to their size. The patch introduces a minimum size of 2M for mTHP folios to be considered for splitting, which can be adjusted later if needed. It also maintains backwards compatibility by exempting PMD-sized folios from this minimum size. The change is made in the fault path and khugepaged mTHP collapse path, with minimal overhead on the common order-0 fault path.

With this, thp_underused_split_page starts counting mTHP splits.
thp_split_page and thp_deferred_split_page count PMD-sized folios only,

series_items.patch_summary: This patch reduces cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists by rearranging the layout of struct mem_cgroup_per_node in memory. The goal is to minimize unnecessary overhead caused by spatial prefetching on Intel CPUs, which can lead to increased lock contention and slower performance. The patch achieves this by moving the 'memcg_pn_cold' group after 'memcg_pn_read_mostly', ensuring that the read-mostly cacheline is paired with the cold cacheline instead of the LRU list heads. This change was validated through benchmarking, which showed a significant reduction in contention and improved performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] memcg: don't go through the lruvec for folio and kmem lruvec stat updates
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory cgroup (memcg) statistics updates by bypassing the lruvec data structure for folio and kmem lruvec stat updates. It directly passes the memcg and node to the mod_memcg_node_state function, reducing contention with other threads that access the lru_lock holder. This change improves throughput in certain scenarios, such as on a 2-socket Skylake system with multiple threads accessing shared memory.

This change improves performance on systems that use spatial prefetching, such as Intel CPUs. The patch includes two changes: one that reorders the fields in struct mem_cgroup_per_node, and another that modifies the stat update functions to skip using the lruvec. The results show a significant improvement in pages per second for threads faulting in and freeing memory in a single memcg.

  its first line can still be paired with the end of the preceding

review_comments.summary: The author addressed Andrew's concern about the effectiveness of rearranging struct mem_cgroup_per_node, explaining that even when the read-mostly line isn't paired with a cold line, it's still not causing significant contention in practice. review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Andrew,

Thanks for taking a look at this series!

The AI review's commentary is correct but it doesn't seem to matter in
practice. In the cases where the read-mostly line isn't paired with
the cold line, it's paired with the line that holds the end of
lru_zone_size[] and the reclaim iterator, which are also rarely
written outside of reclaim so it doesn't see much contention. In my
benchmarking runs, the memcgs are freshly created and contain a mix of
both alignments. Before the changes in this series, the per-memcg
throughput was bimodal depending on the alignment, but afterwards, the
throughput is uniform across memcgs.

Here's an updated version of the "Fix this by moving the memcg_pn_cold
group..." paragraph in patch 1 that mentions this:

Fix this by moving the memcg_pn_cold group, which is only touched when
the memcg is reparented or freed, right after memcg_pn_read_mostly.
SLAB_HWCACHE_ALIGN only aligns objects to a cacheline, and the struct
is 576 bytes, so depending on where an object lands, its read-mostly
cacheline is now paired either with its cold cacheline or with the last
cacheline of the preceding object, which holds the end of
lru_zone_size[] and the reclaim iterator. Both are rarely written
outside of reclaim, so either way the read-mostly cacheline is no
longer paired with the LRU list heads.

Would you be able to swap it in or would you prefer that I send a v4?

Thanks,
Joanne

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch fixes a race condition in the hugetlb_vmemmap code by mapping the shared tail page writable instead of restoring RCU protection. The issue arises when a lockless get reads a non-zero refcount from a page that is then freed and reused as a hugetlb tail page, causing a write fault on read-only vmemmap. The patch also drops the write protect step for bootmem folios optimized in early boot.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author acknowledged that the swapoff path needs to drop the per-vswap spinlock before calling try_to_unmap(), agreed to restructure in v2.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
Date: Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:23:47 +0000
Subject: [PATCH] mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: map the shared tail page writable

page_ref_add_unless_zero() reads the refcount and then updates it with
a cmpxchg.  A lockless get, such as a page cache lookup or a PFN
scanner, can read a non-zero refcount from a page that is then freed
and reused as a hugetlb tail page.  If HVO remaps its struct page to
the shared tail page in between, the cmpxchg writes to read-only
vmemmap:

    CPU0 (lockless get)               CPU1
    c = atomic_read(&page->_refcount)
                                      page freed
                                      page allocated as a hugetlb tail
                                      HVO remaps the struct page RO
    try_cmpxchg(&page->_refcount, &c, c + 1)
      -> write fault on read-only vmemmap

The refcount is zero by then and the compare fails, but LOCK CMPXCHG on
x86 writes anyway.  The kernel oopses when hugetlb pages are allocated
at runtime with HVO enabled while a lockless get races with it.

Commit bd225530a4c7 ("mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: fix race with speculative PFN
walkers") closed the window with RCU on both sides.  The RCU was removed
together with fake heads, on the wrong belief that it was only needed
for them.

Map the shared tail page writable instead of restoring the RCU.  Every
struct page on it is a tail with a zero refcount, so a late cmpxchg
fails and leaves the page unchanged.  RCU would put rcu_read_lock()
back around every get and synchronize_rcu() back into hugetlb
allocation and freeing.

The cost is the protection against stray writes to tail struct pages.
The shared page is shared by all hugetlb folios of the same order in
the zone, so such a write now corrupts all of them instead of oopsing.

Bootmem folios optimized in early boot get their tails mapped writable
and write protected later.  Drop the write protect step.

reviewer notes that the patch may not have caught all potential issues due to a corner case (memory failure) not being encountered during testing, and suggests additional verification is needed

Reviewer Muchun Song noted that without read-only (RO) permissions on the tail page, an invalid write causes massive corruption and silently corrupts memory, making it harder to debug the crash context, but ultimately deemed this loss of debuggability as not critical and suggested restoring RW permissions to solve the race condition.

Possibly, but we indeed didn't catch it during the testing phase.

The likely reason is that we hadn't anticipated issues in a corner
case like a memory failure. Also, it's worth noting that during our
test and verification phases, actual memory failures simply didn't
occur.

---

Under the new schema, an invalid write causes massive corruption,
which would likely result in an immediate and noticeable failure
(like a crash or oops). From a developer's perspective, this
definitely helps us "fail fast" and find the bug quickly.

So, let me think about what we actually lose without RO.

I believe the main difference is the debuggability of the crash context.
With RO, the hardware intercepts the write immediately and throws
a clear page fault with a call trace. Without RO, an invalid write
silently corrupts memory, and we might only find out later with no
clue where it happened.

Of course, losing this debuggability doesn't seem like a critical
issue after all. Thinking about it this way, restoring RW permissions
to fix this race condition seems like an acceptable trade-off.

Therefore, I am kind of leaning towards removing the RO protection
and restoring RW permissions to solve the race.

From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
Date: Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:23:47 +0000
Subject: [PATCH] mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: map the shared tail page writable

page_ref_add_unless_zero() reads the refcount and then updates it with
a cmpxchg.  A lockless get, such as a page cache lookup or a PFN
scanner, can read a non-zero refcount from a page that is then freed
and reused as a hugetlb tail page.  If HVO remaps its struct page to
the shared tail page in between, the cmpxchg writes to read-only
vmemmap:

    CPU0 (lockless get)               CPU1
    c = atomic_read(&page->_refcount)
                                      page freed
                                      page allocated as a hugetlb tail
                                      HVO remaps the struct page RO
    try_cmpxchg(&page->_refcount, &c, c + 1)
      -> write fault on read-only vmemmap

The refcount is zero by then and the compare fails, but LOCK CMPXCHG on
x86 writes anyway.  The kernel oopses when hugetlb pages are allocated
at runtime with HVO enabled while a lockless get races with it.

Commit bd225530a4c7 ("mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: fix race with speculative PFN
walkers") closed the window with RCU on both sides.  The RCU was removed
together with fake heads, on the wrong belief that it was only needed
for them.

Map the shared tail page writable instead of restoring the RCU.  Every
struct page on it is a tail with a zero refcount, so a late cmpxchg
fails and leaves the page unchanged.  RCU would put rcu_read_lock()
back around every get and synchronize_rcu() back into hugetlb
allocation and freeing.

The cost is the protection against stray writes to tail struct pages.
The shared page is shared by all hugetlb folios of the same order in
the zone, so such a write now corrupts all of them instead of oopsing.

Bootmem folios optimized in early boot get their tails mapped writable
and write protected later.  Drop the write protect step.

Fixes: 32c440d67e6c ("mm: drop fake head checks")
Fixes: 01b1d0ffb6f7 ("hugetlb: remove VMEMMAP_SYNCHRONIZE_RCU")

Closes: https://lore.kernel.org/r/ebc7bde1-f52e-4da8-b16f-822d6c0a4d74@kernel.org

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCHv7 13/18] mm: Drop fake head checks
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch fixes a race condition in the hugetlb_vmemmap code by mapping the shared tail page writable instead of restoring RCU protection. The issue arises when a lockless get reads a non-zero refcount from a page that is then freed and reused as a hugetlb tail page, causing a write fault on read-only vmemmap. The patch also drops the write protect step for bootmem folios optimized in early boot.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the protection of shared tail pages in HVO (HugeTLB Vmemmap Optimization), specifically that a stray write to any tail silently corrupts all hugetlb folios of that order in the zone instead of oopsing. The author acknowledges this issue and suggests mapping the shared tail page writable as an alternative solution, which would make the race harmless.
review_comments.raw_body:
Fair enough. Here's some context.

HVO (HugeTLB Vmemmap Optimization) frees most of the memmap of a hugetlb
folio by remapping the struct pages after the first vmemmap page to a
shared page, mapped read-only.

Every lockless get of a page reference (e.g. page cache lookup, PFN
scanners) relies on page_ref_add_unless_zero(), which is
atomic_add_unless(&page->_refcount, nr, 0).

The page can be freed and reused between finding it and the get; the
zero refcount is what makes the get fail. The race:

  lockless get                        other CPU
  c = atomic_read(&page->_refcount)
  c != 0
                                      page freed
                                      page allocated as a hugetlb tail
                                      HVO remaps it read-only
  try_cmpxchg(&page->_refcount, &c, c + nr)
    -> write fault on read-only vmemmap

The refcount is zero by then and the compare fails, but LOCK CMPXCHG
writes anyway.

Before v7.1, HVO mapped the tail vmemmap pages to the head vmemmap page
of the same folio. The first struct page in each of them read as the
head, with PG_head and the head's refcount: a fake head. A get on a fake
head of a folio in use always tried the write, not only in a race, so
page_ref_add_unless() checked for fake heads before the atomic.

Back then, the race above was closed by bd225530a4c7: rcu_read_lock()
around the read and the cmpxchg, and synchronize_rcu() in HVO before the
remap. The refcounts are already zero by then, so the get either
finishes its cmpxchg before the remap or reads zero and bails.

Since v7.1, tails encode the head as a mask instead of a pointer, so
tails of the same order are identical and HVO maps them to one page of
real tails, shared by the zone. Fake heads are gone, and every read-only
struct page is a tail with a zero refcount. The race is not gone, but
32c440d67e6c and 01b1d0ffb6f7 dropped the RCU on both sides anyway, on
the wrong belief that it was only there for fake heads. That is what
David reported.

One fix is to put the RCU back. It works, but it means rcu_read_lock()
around every get that goes through page_ref_add_unless_zero(), GUP-fast
included, and synchronize_rcu() on hugetlb allocation and freeing,
including surplus allocation at fault time. So I am exploring other
options.

The fixup is one of them. With the new layout, a fault on that CMPXCHG
can only be a write to an HVO tail, so the refcount is zero and the get
fails, and the fault only happens in the window above. With GCC the loop
compiles to the same code as before; clang adds a SETE/TEST per call
site.

Writing this, I just realized that we have another option -- map the
shared tail page writable. A failing LOCK CMPXCHG writes back the value
it read, and the get never changes a zero refcount, so the race becomes
harmless. The cost is the protection: the page is shared by every
hugetlb folio of that order in the zone, so a stray write to any tail
silently corrupts all of them instead of oopsing.


And yes, I know, HVO is an ugly hack, like most of hugetlb. But it
works, and it gives back about 16MB of memmap for every 1GB hugetlb
page.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

The likely reason is that we hadn't anticipated issues in a corner
case like a memory failure. Also, it's worth noting that during our
test and verification phases, actual memory failures simply didn't
occur.

Under the new schema, an invalid write causes massive corruption,
which would likely result in an immediate and noticeable failure
(like a crash or oops). From a developer's perspective, this
definitely helps us "fail fast" and find the bug quickly.

So, let me think about what we actually lose without RO.

I believe the main difference is the debuggability of the crash context.
With RO, the hardware intercepts the write immediately and throws
a clear page fault with a call trace. Without RO, an invalid write
silently corrupts memory, and we might only find out later with no
clue where it happened.

Of course, losing this debuggability doesn't seem like a critical
issue after all. Thinking about it this way, restoring RW permissions
to fix this race condition seems like an acceptable trade-off.

Therefore, I am kind of leaning towards removing the RO protection
and restoring RW permissions to solve the race.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
Date: Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:23:47 +0000
Subject: [PATCH] mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: map the shared tail page writable

page_ref_add_unless_zero() reads the refcount and then updates it with
a cmpxchg.  A lockless get, such as a page cache lookup or a PFN
scanner, can read a non-zero refcount from a page that is then freed
and reused as a hugetlb tail page.  If HVO remaps its struct page to
the shared tail page in between, the cmpxchg writes to read-only
vmemmap:

    CPU0 (lockless get)               CPU1
    c = atomic_read(&page->_refcount)
                                      page freed
                                      page allocated as a hugetlb tail
                                      HVO remaps the struct page RO
    try_cmpxchg(&page->_refcount, &c, c + 1)
      -> write fault on read-only vmemmap

The refcount is zero by then and the compare fails, but LOCK CMPXCHG on
x86 writes anyway.  The kernel oopses when hugetlb pages are allocated
at runtime with HVO enabled while a lockless get races with it.

Commit bd225530a4c7 ("mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: fix race with speculative PFN
walkers") closed the window with RCU on both sides.  The RCU was removed
together with fake heads, on the wrong belief that it was only needed
for them.

Map the shared tail page writable instead of restoring the RCU.  Every
struct page on it is a tail with a zero refcount, so a late cmpxchg
fails and leaves the page unchanged.  RCU would put rcu_read_lock()
back around every get and synchronize_rcu() back into hugetlb
allocation and freeing.

The cost is the protection against stray writes to tail struct pages.
The shared page is shared by all hugetlb folios of the same order in
the zone, so such a write now corrupts all of them instead of oopsing.

Bootmem folios optimized in early boot get their tails mapped writable
and write protected later.  Drop the write protect step.

Fixes: 32c440d67e6c ("mm: drop fake head checks")
Fixes: 01b1d0ffb6f7 ("hugetlb: remove VMEMMAP_SYNCHRONIZE_RCU")
Reported-by: David Hildenbrand (Arm) <david@kernel.org>
Closes: https://lore.kernel.org/r/ebc7bde1-f52e-4da8-b16f-822d6c0a4d74@kernel.org
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>

 include/linux/mm.h                 |  2 --
 mm/hugetlb.c                       |  4 ----
 mm/hugetlb_vmemmap.c               | 21 +++++++--------------
 mm/sparse-vmemmap.c                | 23 -----------------------
 5 files changed, 16 insertions(+), 47 deletions(-)

index 9fa8642ded48..6cd85aca4b96 100644

+++ b/Documentation/mm/vmemmap_dedup.rst
@@ -131,8 +131,15 @@ pages of ``struct page`` (page 1 to page 7) are tail pages.
 The optimization is only applied when the size of the struct page is a power
 of 2. In this case, all tail pages of the same order are identical. See
 compound_head(). This allows us to remap the tail pages of the vmemmap to a
-shared, read-only page. The head page is also remapped to a new page. This
-allows the original vmemmap pages to be freed.
+shared page. The head page is also remapped to a new page. This allows the
+original vmemmap pages to be freed.
+
+The shared page is mapped writable. A lockless get of a page reference can
+read a non-zero refcount before the remap and attempt its atomic update
+after it. The refcount of a tail page is zero, so the update fails without
+changing the page. Nothing else may write to the shared page: it is shared
+by all HugeTLB pages of the same size in the zone, and a stray write would
+corrupt all of them.
 
 Here is how things look after remapping::
 
@@ -196,8 +203,6 @@ happens at a later stage when we populate the sections. HugeTLB reuses the
 the head vmemmap page representing, whereas device-dax reuses the tail
 vmemmap page. This results in only half of the savings compared to HugeTLB.
 
-Deduplicated tail pages are not mapped read-only.

 Here's how things look like on device-dax after the sections are populated::
 
  +-----------+ ---virt_to_page---> +-----------+   mapping to   +-----------+

-		 * Remap the tail pages as read-only to catch illegal write

-		entry = mk_pte(walk->vmemmap_tail, PAGE_KERNEL_RO);
+		entry = mk_pte(walk->vmemmap_tail, PAGE_KERNEL);
 	}
 
 	list_add(&page->lru, walk->vmemmap_pages);
@@ -629,19 +631,10 @@ static void __hugetlb_vmemmap_optimize_folios(struct hstate *h,
 	nr_to_optimize = 0;
 	list_for_each_entry(folio, folio_list, lru) {
 		int ret;
-		unsigned long spfn, epfn;
 
-		if (boot && folio_test_hugetlb_vmemmap_optimized(folio)) {
-			/*
-			 * Already optimized by pre-HVO, just map the
-			 * mirrored tail page structs RO.
-			 */
-			spfn = (unsigned long)&folio->page;
-			epfn = spfn + hugetlb_vmemmap_size(h);
-			vmemmap_wrprotect_hvo(spfn, epfn, folio_nid(folio),
-					HUGETLB_VMEMMAP_RESERVE_SIZE);
+		/* Already optimized by pre-HVO */
+		if (boot && folio_test_hugetlb_vmemmap_optimized(folio))
 			continue;
-		}
 
 		nr_to_optimize++;

index 5a2469fb1838..3f25d4a0bf47 100644
--- a/mm/sparse-vmemmap.c
+++ b/mm/sparse-vmemmap.c
@@ -299,29 +299,6 @@ int __meminit vmemmap_populate_basepages(unsigned long start, unsigned long end,
 	return vmemmap_populate_range(start, end, node, altmap, -1, 0);
 }

> Right, that is by design.
> 
> defrag_mode keeps the free space in unmovable and reclaimable blocks for
> those allocations, so they don't spill into movable blocks. Your 64K

the major cause of fragmentation nicely, but the assumption is that compaction
is a free resource, unfortunately on smaller devices that's not the case.

It also removes the wrapper function swap_cluster_info_dynamic and merges the two cluster arrays into si->cluster_info. As a result, swap clusters are no longer destroyed when they empty, but instead wait to be reused like physical devices' clusters.

It lays the groundwork for subsequent patches that will implement allocation paths and backends for the virtual swap layer.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 02/12] mm, swap: support zswap and zero-filled swap pages as vswap backends
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for zswap and zero-filled swap pages as vswap backends, allowing users to use zswap without a physical backing swapfile. It introduces new logic for reclaim and overcommit, including the addition of mem_cgroup_can_swap() to determine if an anonymous page can be swapped out, and updates the OVERCOMMIT_GUESS heuristic to account for vswap-backed entries. The patch also disables THP swapin for vswap entries and modifies zswap writeback behavior when vswap is enabled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 03/12] mm, swap: prepare the swap IO path for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the swap IO path for vswap by allowing it to submit IO for a swap entry other than folio->swap. It introduces a new sector calculation function, swap_entry_sector, and updates various functions to use this new function instead of swap_folio_sector. The patch also adds a 'nofs' flag to the swap_io_ctx structure to carry reclaim's NOFS restriction in the I/O context. This change is necessary for adding a physical swap backend for vswap. There are no functional changes as all callers currently pass folio->swap.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 04/12] mm, swap: support physical swap as a vswap backend
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for physical swap as a backend for the virtual swap layer, allowing pages to be swapped out directly to physical memory when zswap declines them. The physical slot is tracked via a vswap-tagged swap_table entry on the physical cluster, and swapoff reads each vswap entry back through its rmap slot before freeing the physical slot. If zswap is disabled or the folio's cgroup is at its zswap limit, the folio gets a physical swap slot directly, bypassing vswap.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 05/12] mm, swap: enable THP swapin for vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enables transparent huge page (THP) swapin for vswap entries, allowing large anonymous folios to be swapped in as a unit when their vswap entries share contiguous physical swap slots on a synchronous IO device. This improves performance by reducing the number of faults and retries required during the swap process. The patch checks the backing type of vswap entries and rejects batches with non-THP-amenable backings, such as uniformly ZSWAP or mixed-backing. If the backing is THP-amenable, the folio is swapped in at its original order; otherwise, the fault retries at a smaller order.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 06/12] mm, swap: write back vswap zswap entries to physical swap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for writing back zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap. It mirrors the existing zswap writeback path, but allocates the backing physical slot on demand at writeback time instead of pre-allocating it. The zswap shrinker now skips vswap entries when out of physical swap space. This change allows vswap entries to be written back to physical swap, which was previously not possible.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 07/12] mm, swap: reclaim physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a memory management issue where physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries are not being reclaimed when swap space is scarce. The problem arises because the existing put-time reclaim mechanism does not reliably recover these slots, leading to wasted capacity for new allocations. To solve this, the patch introduces a new reclaim strategy that targets such slots once swap usage exceeds 50%. This approach aims to free up physical capacity by reaping redundant backing storage associated with vswap entries that have dropped out of the swap cache.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 08/12] mm, swap: only charge physical swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies how swap entries are charged against a memory control group (memcg). Instead of charging memcg->swap when a virtual swap entry is allocated, it charges only when the entry acquires physical backing. This change affects what the counter means and when the charge can fail, allowing for more accurate accounting and reclaiming of anon memory even with memory.swap.max set to 0 if zswap is allowed. The patch also refactors the swap memcg operations into separate helpers for getting, recording, charging, uncharging, and putting the owner.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 09/12] mm, swap: add debugfs counters for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two debugfs counters to track virtual swap usage in the Linux kernel. The first counter, 'used', tracks the number of virtual swap slots (pages) currently allocated. The second counter, 'alloc_reject', counts the cumulative number of pages whose vswap slot allocation failed. These counters are exposed under the '/sys/kernel/debug/vswap/' directory and can be used for debugging purposes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces Virtual Swap Space, a feature that allows for virtual swap space allocation within the Linux kernel. It enables the use of zswap (a compressed block device) as a backing store for virtual swap space, allowing for more efficient use of physical memory and reducing the need for traditional swap partitions. The patches include various cleanups, bug fixes, and improvements to existing code, including changes to cgroup memory statistics and sysctl parameters. The goal is to provide a flexible and scalable solution for managing swap space in modern Linux systems.
